analysis.one_liner: Bans states from setting stricter standards on farm products made in other states.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Agriculture Committee; with 9 cosponsors, it got no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop any state or local government from imposing a standard or condition on an agricultural product that was produced in another state, unless that rule already exists in federal law or in the state where the product was made [S2][S3]. In practice, that means a state whose voters passed a stricter rule — for example, requiring larger cages for egg-laying hens — could no longer apply it to eggs shipped in from other states [S2]. The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 114th Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Producers of agricultural products — especially large livestock, egg, and poultry operations — who want to sell into states with stricter production rules without having to meet those rules. A single federal-floor production process could be sold nationwide, including into states whose own voters chose higher standards.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits states and localities from imposing any standard or condition on agricultural products produced in another state that goes beyond federal law and the laws of the producing state [S2][S3].
Covers any 'agricultural product' as defined by the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946, a broad category of farm goods [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Residents of states that adopted stricter standards, whose rules would no longer reach out-of-state goods, and the state governments whose regulatory authority is stripped. Voters who passed standards by ballot initiative, such as cage-free egg requirements, would lose the practical effect of their vote.

drawbacks.text: It strips state regulatory power: a state could no longer enforce standards its own citizens adopted when the products come from elsewhere, hollowing out ballot initiatives and state food and animal-welfare rules [S2][S3].

The industry's good-faith argument is real: a patchwork of differing state standards can raise compliance costs and prices — the reason federal preemption is often proposed — but this bill resolves the patchwork by eliminating the stricter standards rather than by raising the federal floor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow to producers who avoid the cost of meeting individual states' stricter rules; its costs fall on states and their voters, who lose the standards they enacted, and on consumers in those states. It lowers the floor rather than raising it. The bill never advanced, so the tradeoff was never tested in legislation.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and then to its Livestock subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended in January 2017 — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Steve King (R-IA) introduced the bill on February 3, 2015, joined as original cosponsors by Reps. Rouzer, Neugebauer, Peterson, Blum, Huelskamp, and Young of Iowa [S3].
It ended the Congress with 9 cosponsors: 8 Republicans and 1 Democrat [S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Agriculture on February 3, 2015, and to the Subcommittee on Livestock and Foreign Agriculture on February 27, 2015; no further action was taken [S5].
The bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote, and expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, state governments and their voters kept the authority to enforce their own production standards, and animal-welfare rules states had adopted remained fully enforceable. Producers gained no new federal shield from those rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States and their voters kept their standards

industries.industry: Industrial livestock, egg, and poultry producers
industries.note: The bill would let these producers sell into states with stricter standards without meeting them, ending the cost of separate production lines for different states. The tradeoff is that standards those states' voters adopted would no longer apply to most goods sold there.
The bill strips state and local authority to set standards on agricultural products produced elsewhere, beyond federal law and the producing state's own rules.

industries.industry: Producers already complying with stricter state standards
industries.note: Farms that invested in meeting a state's higher standards, such as cage-free requirements, would face competitors shipping in goods made under weaker rules.
